introduction.p: A definite integral with fixed endpoints gives one accumulated amount. But if the upper endpoint moves, the accumulated amount changes. That changing amount is a function.

This is the same idea as recovering position from velocity. At each time, the position change is the accumulated signed velocity up to that time. If we know the velocity graph, that change is an area-with-sign whose right endpoint moves. An odometer instead accumulates speed, so its reading never decreases.

exercise.title: Why does a moving endpoint turn an integral into a function?

statement.p: A definite integral with both endpoints fixed is a single number. In your own words, why does letting the upper endpoint move produce a function A(x), and why is that the same idea as an odometer reading built from a velocity graph?

hint.p: At each time, the odometer stores one accumulated amount. Changing the stopping time changes that amount, so the stored totals form a function of the stopping time.

exercise.title: What is the letter inside the integral doing?

statement.p: The book writes A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt rather than using x both as the endpoint and as the letter inside the integral. In your own words, why is t a temporary placeholder, and why is the endpoint x not temporary?

hint.p: The input to A is the stopping point of the accumulation. The letter that names the variable of integration is only a dummy that can be renamed.

exercise.title: Why is the change in accumulated area a thin new strip?

statement.p: Additivity gives A(x+h)-A(x)=\int_x^{x+h} f(t)\,dt. In your own words, why is that identity the key to the slope of A, and why should the difference quotient approach the current height f(x) when f is continuous?

hint.p: The new strip has width h. For small h, nearby heights are close to f(x), so the average height of the strip is close to the height at x.

statement.p: If f(t)\ge0 and x<a, then A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt can still be negative. In your own words, why does the sign come from the direction of accumulation rather than from the height of the graph?
